extraction.name: Common Corpus: The Largest Collection of Ethical Data for LLM Pre-Training
extraction.description: Common Corpus is the largest open dataset for language model pre-training, comprising about two trillion tokens. It includes uncopyrighted or permissibly licensed data from diverse sources and domains, covering a wide variety of languages from main European to low-resource ones, and a large portion of code data. The dataset provides detailed provenance, filtering, and curation, aiming to be a critical infrastructure for open science research in LLMs, compliant with data security regulations.
extraction.license: The data assembled in Common Corpus are either uncopyrighted or under permissible licenses, allowing use for any purpose without asking for permission. Specific licenses include Public Domain, CC-By, MIT, CC-By-SA, Apache-2.0, BSD-3-Clause, Open license, BSD-2-Clause, CC-BY-4.0, and CC0-1.0. Each data object includes license information for filtering.
extraction.creator: Pierre-Carl Langlais, Carlos Rosas Hinostroza, Mattia Nee, Catherine Amett, Pavel Chizhov, Eliot Krzystof Jones, Irène Girard, David Mach, Anastasia Stasenko, Ivan P. Yamshchikov
extraction.inLanguage: English, French, German, Spanish, Latin, Italian, Polish, Greek, Portuguese, Russian, Dutch, Luxembourgish, Danish, Swedish, Serbian, Czech, Arabic, Bengali, Persian, Sanskrit, Urdu, Chinese, Korean, Bulgarian, Romanian, Latvian, Lithuanian, Croatian, Estonian, Hungarian, Finnish, Slovak, Slovenian, Maltese, Tigrinya, Farsi, Albanian, Kurdish, Pushto, Irish, Norwegian, Icelandic, Dari, Armenian, Japanese, M¯ aori, and over 300 languages from Wikidata.
extraction.isLiveDataset: Yes, Common Corpus will remain an evolving resource reflecting the need for a continuous open infrastructure, with HuggingFace ensuring a proper archiving of past versions for reproducibility.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The data collection process involved aggregating content that is either uncopyrighted or under permissible licenses. It includes data from diverse sources like government documents, cultural heritage institutions (using Collections As Data, APIs, and standard retrieval methods), scientific papers (from OpenAlex and arXiv), code repositories (The Stack v1 and v2 from GitHub), web sources (Wikimedia projects, YouTube Commons, StackExchange), and semantic data (Wikidata). An internal rights verification process was implemented for cultural heritage content, following specific criteria including author life, data object creation time, and institutional location (US or EU). The multilingual part of the dataset was never machine-translated, and efforts were made to increase diversity and involve local communities to identify relevant data sources.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Document analysis, Software Collection, Web Scraping, Web API, User-generated content data, Others
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data sources include: Open Government (SEC annual reports, WTO official documents, AMF documents, TED EU Tenders, GATT Library documents, Europarl, Caselaw Access Project, CourtListener, EUR-lex, Eurovoc, French administrative bodies' websites, USPTO, UN Digital Library, EU websites, OECD); Open Culture (Collections As Data, Internet Archive, Delpher, Chronicle America, Europeana, Gallica, Biblioteca, LoC Books, US PD Newspapers, New Zealand PD Newspapers, German Digital Library, Mannheim Corpus of Historical Newspapers and Magazines, Biblioteca Digital Hispánica, Koninklijke Bibliotheek, National Library of Luxembourg); Open Science (OpenAlex, arXiv); Open Code (The Stack v1 and v2 from GitHub); Open Web (Wikipedia, Wikisource, YouTube Commons audio transcripts, StackExchange from The Pile); Open Semantic (Wikidata).
extraction.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: The dataset development has been an ongoing effort since May 2023, with the first version published in March 2024, and the current version released in February 2025. For Finance Commons, documents span from the mid-20th century to 2024. Open Culture datasets include historical content from the 18th-19th centuries or even earlier.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Data manipulation includes the synthetic rewriting of documents to remove harmful language, as performed by the Celadon toxicity classifier. PII is replaced with fictitious but realistic values rather than being removed or partially anonymized.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The preprocessing pipeline includes: Text Segmentation (using the custom-developed Segmentext tool); OCR Error Detection (using OCRoscope and OCRerrcr); OCR Correction (using the custom-developed OCRonos model); PII Removal (identifying and replacing Personally Identifiable Information using Microsoft’s Presidio tool, enhanced with custom regular expression patterns); Toxicity Detection and Filtering (using the multilingual toxicity classifier Celadon to identify and filter/rewrite content along five dimensions); Code Data Filtering (removing files not in desired languages/formats, filtering by permissible licenses, applying manual filters for low-quality data, removing files with 75% or more digits, and normalizing newline sequences); Wikidata Processing (translating items and properties into formal natural language sequences without textual synthesis).
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The multilingual toxicity classifier, Celadon, was trained from scratch on 2 million annotated samples to identify toxic and harmful content along five dimensions: race and origin-based bias, gender and sexuality-based bias, religious bias, ability bias, and violence and abuse. The training dataset for Celadon was released as part of a separate work.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Segmentext (for text segmentation), OCRoscope (for OCR error detection), OCRerrcr (for OCR error detection), OCRonos (for OCR correction), Microsoft’s Presidio (for PII removal), Celadon (for toxicity detection and filtering), and potentially a language model for fine-grained curation and annotation of web archives.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: Common Corpus is designed as an evolving resource and continuous open infrastructure. HuggingFace ensures proper archiving of past versions for reproducibility. Future plans include collecting more data in European languages (LLMs4EU project) and enlarging corpora in African languages (e.g., Swahili, Wolof, Bambara).
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Personally Identifiable Information (PII) is identified and replaced with fictitious but realistic values using Microsoft’s Presidio tool to comply with legislation such as GDPR. The dataset aims to not capture highly sensitive data.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: Common Corpus is a significant contribution to the open LLM research community, supporting the pre-training of fully open and auditable LLMs while adhering to legal and regulatory norms. It is part of the Current AI initiative, aiming to accelerate the development of open AI building blocks that serve and are shaped by the public interest. It was built with support from AI Alliance, LANGU:IA (French Ministry of Culture and DINUM), Wikimedia Enterprise, Wikimedia Germany, Genci, Scaleway, Tracto AI, Mozilla, HuggingFace, Occiglot, and Eleuther AI.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset addresses potential biases and harms. Historical texts, particularly from the Open Culture collection (e.g., 18th-19th century periodicals and monographs), may contain harmful language due to changed cultural norms regarding ethnic groups, women, violence, etc. To mitigate this, a multilingual toxicity classifier, Celadon, was developed to identify and filter/rewrite content along five dimensions: race and origin-based bias, gender and sexuality-based bias, religious bias, ability bias, and violence and abuse. Web data is also acknowledged as a major source of harmful and biased content (e.g., sexual content, hate speech, racial/gender biases in Common Crawl).
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Known limitations include: The corpus is not exhaustive and is far from collecting the whole range of available open data (the 'open data paradox'); while language diversity is large, coverage for low-resource languages is still shallow; the current amount of data (2 trillion tokens) is suitable for pre-training models of limited size but insufficient for larger models; the dataset does not contain data for instruction-tuning or specialized tasks, making it not directly suitable for task-specific fine-tuning; curation methods, including toxicity detection and PII removal, are not 100% accurate; OCR errors, despite correction efforts, present considerable challenges to models; struggles with accurate license identification in web archives.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is primarily intended for language model pre-training. It can be used on its own or in conjunction with existing open datasets. Specific use cases include: Training models for creative writing; developing historical language models; developing vision-language models (VLMs) for advanced document segmentation and processing; developing language models with legal knowledge and for document processing in official administrative applications; training models for coding applications or to improve natural language reasoning, world knowledge, mathematics, and structured output tasks; creating a wider range of language model artifacts, including multimodal datasets, classifiers, synthetic datasets, and benchmarks; opening opportunities for the creation of ethical fine-tuning datasets (e.g., for RAG models).
